title: Task decomposition patterns: chaining, routing, parallelization and orchestrator-workers

units.text: Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
What you will be able to do
Choose between prompt chaining, routing, parallelization and orchestrator-workers based on whether the subtasks are known in advance
Assign a model to each decomposed subtask based on how hard and how frequent it is
Decompose a multi-dimension task into Agent SDK subagents with scoped tools and descriptions
Recognise when a tight loop of tool calls should move into code through programmatic tool calling
Key concept
Task decomposition

Splitting one hard request into smaller subtasks, each handled by its own focused model call, prompt, tool set or model. The design question is who decides the subtasks: you, while you build the system, or a model, at run time.
In this lesson
Why decomposition improves results
Prompt chaining: fixed steps with gates between them
Routing: split by input type, and match the model to the subtask
Parallelization: sectioning and voting

Why decomposition improves results

One model call that has to do everything gives each part of the job less attention. If a single prompt has to screen a request for unsafe content and also answer it, both jobs get worse. Splitting the work so that each call handles one consideration is the basic move behind every pattern on this page. Decomposition fits best where several well-scoped tasks feed one overall goal.
The patterns differ in
who decides the subtasks

. In prompt chaining, routing and parallelization, the designer fixes the subtasks when the system is built. In orchestrator-workers, a model works them out at run time for each input. This is the same line drawn in
Workflows versus agents
, seen here as a decomposition choice: if you can list the subtasks today, write them into code. If they depend on the input, let a model plan them.
Decomposition is not free. Every extra call adds latency and tokens, and every handoff is a place where context can get lost. Each pattern below says what it costs and when that cost is worth paying.
Checkpoint 1 of 10
Check yourself

A support assistant uses one prompt to screen each request for unsafe content and also answer it. Both the screening and the answers are mediocre. The team moves screening into its own call, separate from the call that answers. Why should this improve results?
Splitting lets a model decide at run time which subtasks each request needs.
Each call handles one consideration and gives it full attention, so both screening and answering get better.
Shorter prompts mean the split design uses fewer tokens in total than the single call did.
Each smaller call returns sooner, so the system as a whole responds faster.

Prompt chaining: fixed steps with gates between them
Prompt chaining

splits a task into a fixed sequence of steps. Each model call takes the previous call's output as its input. Between steps you can add programmatic checks, called gates, that confirm the process is still on track before the next call runs. Two standard examples: writing marketing copy and then translating it, or writing an outline, checking it against criteria, and only then writing the document.
Predict first
A team turns one long extraction prompt into a four-step chain. What should they expect to happen to latency and accuracy?
Latency falls and accuracy stays the same, because the steps can overlap
Latency rises and accuracy improves, because each call has an easier job
Both improve, because each call is smaller
Chaining fits when a task splits
cleanly into fixed subtasks

. A worked case: turning a quarterly performance summary into a table takes four calls. The first extracts each metric with its value. The second converts the values to one format. The third sorts them in descending order. The fourth renders a markdown table. Each step is trivial for the model, and a code check between steps (for example, "did step 1 return every metric?") catches a failure before it spreads to the later steps.
The same shape appears in Claude Code dynamic workflows. The first agent call returns a list of files in a declared schema, and that list drives the next step, which audits each file.
A two-step workflow: one agent call produces a structured file list, the next step audits each file
javascript
Exam trap
Splitting a prompt into a chain makes the system faster because each call is smaller.
Why is that wrong?

Routing: split by input type, and match the model to the subtask
Routing

classifies an input first, then sends it to a follow-up step built for that category. That step can use its own prompt, its own tools or its own model. The reason to route is interference. If one prompt has to serve every kind of input, tuning it for one kind tends to make it worse for the others. A customer-service system might route general questions, refund requests and technical support into three separate processes, each with its own prompt and tools.
Routing works when the categories really are distinct and
classification can be done accurately
, whether by an LLM or by a traditional classifier. If inputs are often misclassified, every downstream specialist receives work it was not built for.

Routing is also the place to choose a model for each subtask. Model classes differ mainly in how hard a problem they can reliably handle and what that capability costs in price and speed. Easy, common requests go to a small, cheap model. Hard or unusual ones go to a more capable model. Take a support pipeline with two subtasks: classifying a large stream of tickets, and drafting detailed remediation plans for the few that need engineering. Classification goes to Haiku. Remediation, which is multi-step and often new, goes to a more capable class such as Opus. Running everything on the largest model pays its price for every routine classification. Running everything on Haiku asks it to carry work beyond what it reliably handles. Assigning models at random is not routing, because nothing about the input decides where it goes. The broader trade-offs are covered in
model selection trade-offs

With agents, routing means sending work to a specialist agent rather than a specialist prompt. In the Agent SDK, each subagent definition has an optional
field, so a cheap classifier and an expensive drafter can live in the same system.
Checkpoint 3 of 10
Check yourself
Logs from a routed customer-service system show that many refund requests are being sent to the technical-support process, and answers on those tickets are poor. What should the team fix first?
Make the classification step more accurate, because each specialist only works well on the inputs it was built for
Move every specialist process to a more capable model such as Opus so it can cope with misrouted tickets
Add more categories so that each specialist handles a narrower slice of tickets
Merge the three processes back into one prompt that is tuned to handle every ticket type
Checkpoint 4 of 10
Exam question

A support-automation pipeline is decomposed into two subtasks: classifying a high volume of incoming tickets, and drafting detailed technical remediation plans for the subset that need engineering follow-up. How should model selection be applied across these decomposed subtasks?
Assign Claude Haiku 4.5 to the high-volume classification subtask and Claude Opus 4.8 to the remediation subtask, matching model to complexity
Run every subtask on Claude Opus 4.8 with effort set low for classification so remediation drafting still receives full model capability
Run every subtask on Claude Haiku 4.5 and compensate for remediation quality with longer prompts containing extra worked examples
Alternate models randomly between subtasks on every request to average out cost and latency across the decomposed pipeline

Parallelization: sectioning and voting
Parallelization
runs several model calls at the same time and combines their outputs in code. It comes in two forms that solve different problems.
Sectioning

splits a task into independent subtasks that run side by side. For example, one instance answers the user while another screens the request for inappropriate content. This tends to beat one call doing both. Automated evals can also be sectioned, with each call grading a different aspect of the output.
Voting

runs the same task several times and combines the answers to get more confidence. For example, several prompts review the same code for vulnerabilities and flag it if any of them find a problem. Content moderation can also use different vote thresholds to balance false positives against false negatives.
Predict first
A research system fans a question out to five parallel subagents instead of one agent working alone. What is the main thing it gains?
Faster completion, because work runs at the same time
More thorough coverage of the question, usually with more tokens and often more total time
Lower total cost, because each subagent's context is smaller

Speed and cost need to be kept apart. Independent subtasks that run concurrently finish in the time of the slowest one, not the sum of all of them, so a single sectioned step takes less wall-clock time. Across a whole multi-agent system the picture is different. Such systems typically use 3 to 10 times more tokens than one agent, and they often take longer overall because there is so much more computation. Choose parallelization for coverage or confidence, and expect a larger bill.
Exam trap
The main reason to run agents in parallel is to finish sooner and spend less.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 5 of 10
Check yourself

Three separate prompts each review the same pull request for security vulnerabilities at the same time. Code then flags the pull request if any one of them reports a problem. Which decomposition pattern is this, and why?
Voting, because the same task runs several times and the answers are combined for more confidence
Sectioning, because each prompt is an independent subtask running side by side with the others
Prompt chaining, because each review's findings feed into the final flagging decision
Orchestrator-workers, because several model calls run and a final step merges their outputs
Sources
Orchestrator-workers: decomposition decided at run time
In
orchestrator-workers

, a central model reads the task, decides which subtasks it needs, hands each one to a worker model, and combines the results. It can look like sectioning, but the subtasks are not pre-defined. The orchestrator chooses them for each input. A coding change is the standard case: you cannot know in advance how many files need editing or what each edit is.
A lead agent breaks the query into facets at run time, workers research them concurrently, and the lead synthesises
python

That flexibility has costs. Each run makes N+1 calls: one to the orchestrator and one per worker. The decomposition is only as good as the orchestrator's plan, so the orchestrator prompt is where most of the engineering effort goes. Cost can be managed by splitting models, with a capable model such as Opus planning and Haiku workers executing. Do not use the pattern for simple single-output tasks, for latency-critical paths, or when the subtasks are always the same. In that last case, pre-defined parallelization does the job with less machinery.
Claude Managed Agents provides this as
dynamic workflows

. The agent writes a program that runs many agents in phases and combines their results, and the server runs it in the background. Audits, migrations, deep research and cross-checking are the typical uses. Every agent in a run uses tokens, so set a session budget.

Decomposing into Agent SDK subagents
In the Claude Agent SDK, decomposition takes the form of
subagents
. You define them with the
option in code, or as markdown files in

. The main agent invokes them through the Agent tool. Each subagent runs in its own conversation, and its intermediate tool calls stay inside that conversation; only its final message returns to the parent. That isolation is the reason
Coordinator pattern and isolated subagent context
applies even when nothing runs in parallel. The main reason to split may be to keep pages of tool output out of the main agent's context.
The Python AgentDefinition: a required description and prompt, plus optional tool and model scoping
python
Three fields carry the decomposition.
is a natural-language statement of when to use the agent, and the orchestrator reads it to decide where each piece of work goes.
is the allowed list; if you leave it out, the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents, so leaving it blank removes the scoping.
is the specialist's system prompt.

Take a codebase audit with three dimensions (security vulnerabilities, code quality and test coverage), each needing different tools and a different focus. The decomposition is an orchestrator plus three subagents, each with a description and a tool set matched to its dimension. A security scanner, a style checker and a coverage checker can then run at the same time instead of one after another. Compare the alternatives:
One prompt asking the main agent to do all three in sequence.
Every dimension's tool output builds up in a single context, and quality drops as the context grows.
One MCP server exposing all the checks as tools for the main agent.
This adds tools without separating anything. An agent loaded with tools across unrelated domains confuses which domain applies, and with roughly 20 or more tools it struggles to pick the right one.
A larger context window plus extended thinking.
More room does not solve the problem. Response quality can degrade as context grows, so more space for clutter makes the clutter worse.
Checkpoint 7 of 10
Check yourself

Your team is building an agent to audit a codebase for security vulnerabilities, code quality and test coverage. Each of the three needs different tools. In early trials the main agent's context fills up with scanner and linter output, and its later findings get worse. Which design fixes this?
Use an orchestrator plus three subagents, each with its own description, prompt and tool set, so only their final reports go back to the main agent
Put all the checks on one MCP server so the main agent can call any of them as tools
Move to a model with a larger context window and turn on extended thinking so the output fits
Keep one agent but tell it in the prompt to do the three dimensions one after another
Checkpoint 8 of 10
Exam question

A team is building an agent that must audit a large codebase across three distinct dimensions: security vulnerabilities, code quality, and test coverage. Each dimension requires a different set of tools and a different area of focus. Which approach best decomposes this problem using the Agent SDK?
Define an orchestrator agent that invokes specialized subagents through the Agent tool, each configured with a scoped tool set and description matching its subtask domain
Send one prompt to the main agent instructing it to sequentially perform code quality checks, then security scanning, then test coverage analysis without additional configuration
Configure a single MCP server that exposes security, quality, and coverage checks as three separate tools, and let the primary agent call each tool directly instead of delegating
Increase the primary agent's context window and rely on extended thinking so it can reason through all three review dimensions within one continuous session

Moving a tight tool loop into code

Sometimes the cost is in the tool calls, not in the subtasks. If a step needs dozens of small tool calls in a loop, each standard tool-use turn is a round trip through the model, and each result adds to the context.
Programmatic tool calling
removes that overhead. Claude writes code that calls your tools inside a code execution container, so the loop runs in the container instead of passing through the model on every call.
Checking budget compliance for 20 employees takes 20 lookups. How do the standard approach and programmatic tool calling differ?
The savings come from filtering. Data is processed before it reaches the model's context window, so latency and token use both fall. The feature needs the code execution tool at version
or later.
Two other options look similar but do not help. The
Message Batches API

processes requests asynchronously and independently, and most batches finish within an hour. That suits bulk work that does not need an immediate response, but it cannot feed one tool's result into the next step of a live loop.
Wrapping each tool call in its own subagent
keeps the orchestrator's context clean, but it adds a whole agent for each call, and multi-agent setups typically use 3 to 10 times more tokens. That makes the overhead problem worse.
On the exam

Match the remedy to the problem. If the overhead comes from many small tool calls inside one step, use programmatic tool calling. If it comes from unrelated work piling up in one context, use subagents. If the work is bulk and nothing waits on the answer, use batches.
Exam trap
Putting a tight loop of small tool calls into a Message Batches request removes the per-call overhead.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 9 of 10
Check yourself

An expense agent has to make 40 small lookup calls in a loop inside one step. Each call is a round trip through the model, and every result adds to the context. Four fixes are proposed. Which one would make the overhead worse instead of better?
Wrap each lookup in its own subagent so the orchestrator's context only receives each subagent's final message
Filter the lookup results in code before they reach the model, so it reasons over a few lines instead of every row
Have Claude write code that runs all 40 lookups in a code execution container and returns only the rows that matter
Move the loop out of the model's turns so one script makes the calls and passes along only a short summary
Checkpoint 10 of 10
Exam question

A decomposed data-processing workflow requires Claude to invoke dozens of small tools in a tight loop, and issuing each call through the standard conversational tool-use turn is adding significant latency and token overhead. Which technique addresses this?
Use programmatic tool calling so Claude invokes tools directly from a code execution container, cutting round trips and token overhead per call
Wrap each tool invocation in its own subagent so the orchestrator only sees final results, reducing calls the primary agent must track
Batch all tool calls into a single Message Batches request so the many small invocations execute asynchronously outside the conversation
Increase the effort parameter on the primary model so it plans calls further in advance and needs fewer conversational turns to finish
